title: East Coast Begins Massive Cleanup After Historic Thanksgiving Storms Leave Hundreds of Thousands in the Dark
snippet: Millions of residents along the Eastern Seaboard are recovering from a destructive holiday storm system that brought record coastal flooding, 70 mph winds, and forced an unprecedented delay to the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.
content:
Millions across the East Coast spent Friday assessing damage and cleaning up debris after a relentless Thanksgiving Day storm battered the region with 70 mph wind gusts, torrential rains, and destructive coastal flooding.

As of Friday afternoon, nearly 500,000 utility customers remained without power, with the vast majority of outages concentrated in Pennsylvania. The powerful storm system toppled power lines, uprooted trees, and paralyzed travel across several states from North Carolina to Massachusetts.

Historic Flooding and Delayed Holiday Traditions

The severe weather delivered historic high tides to coastal communities. Cape May, New Jersey, recorded its highest tide on record at 9.41 feet, while Atlantic City saw water levels surge to 8.28 feet—the highest tide recorded in the city since Superstorm Sandy in 2012.

The ferocious winds also forced officials to postpone the iconic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City, marking the first time in the event's 100-year history that the parade was delayed due to weather conditions. Organizers rescheduled the parade for Saturday morning, where lighter winds and milder temperatures in the upper 40s are expected.

Emergency Declarations and Heavy Rainfall

Farther south, heavy rain caused severe localized flooding. Parts of eastern Virginia and North Carolina received 3 to 5 inches of rainfall, while Emerald Isle along North Carolina's Southern Outer Banks was inundated with up to 9 inches.

In response to the widespread damage, Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger declared a state of emergency on Friday to bolster recovery operations. "State agencies continue to work closely with local governments and utility partners to restore power to impacted Virginians, maintain safe travel conditions, and support our neighbors," Spanberger said in a statement.

Looking Ahead to the Weekend

While all wind advisories expired Friday afternoon, forecasters warned that minor coastal flooding remains a risk for parts of the Northeast. Rain showers and high-elevation Appalachian snow are expected to taper off heading into Saturday.

However, relief may be short-lived. National weather forecasts indicate a new storm system developing in the Midwest will push east on Sunday, threatening the Ohio Valley, Deep South, and eventually the East Coast with heavy rain and thunderstorms early next week.
